about: skill-authoring vs skill-fitness: the corpus's top-ranked pair by similarity (0.088) and its
most mutual by coverage (0.149 / 0.177), and the one boundary this repo drew on purpose - the
measuring was split out of the authoring skill rather than growing inside it. Until now the
split was argued and never measured, which is the thing this skill exists to object to.
The contested region is narrow and real. skill-authoring claims 'how to word a description so
it triggers on real requests without stealing another skill's'; skill-fitness claims 'why a
skill never fires or fires on the wrong requests' and scoring a candidate description. So a
request about a description that is not working could plausibly go either way, and the intended
line is diagnosis against composition: finding out whether a description works is fitness,
deciding what it should say is authoring.
The last two cases are should-not-steal rather than should-not-trigger: a meta-skill that wins
an ordinary request is a worse failure than one that loses a contested one, and a suite of
positives alone cannot see it.
RESULT 2026-08-31, 10 cases x 3 runs against the installed set: 9/10, and precision 1.0 for
every skill - not one cross-steal in 30 runs, including case 6, written to be the most likely
to go wrong. The split holds. The single failure is case 4, where nothing fired at all, three
times out of three: 'grown to cover three different things ... worth breaking up' shares no
vocabulary with the description's 'deciding whether an over-scoped skill should be split'.
Recall 0.75 for skill-fitness and 0.83 for skill-authoring, both from silence rather than from
losing to each other.
FIX 2026-08-31: a candidate description carrying the request's own vocabulary - 'grown too big,
or covers several different things at once, should be broken up or split' - took case 4 from
0/3 to 2/3, and the candidate name won both fires while the incumbent won none of them. It took
nothing from cases 1-3, which the incumbent kept 3/3 each. Adopted on that split, which is the
adoption rule exactly: wins what the incumbent lost, loses nothing the incumbent won.
VERIFIED 2026-08-31 against the installed set after the change landed, which is the number that
settles it: 10/10, precision 1.0 everywhere, and skill-authoring went to 12/12 - so the longer
skill-fitness description took nothing from its nearest neighbour, the risk a description change
carries. Case 4 shipped at 2/3, the same as its candidate score rather than better: a candidate
figure is a lower bound, not a promise of uplift.
Case 9 came back 2/3 here having been 3/3 twice before, with the third run firing nothing.
Nothing in this change touches invoke-task-conventions, so read it as run-to-run variance - a
2/3 is a pass and not a clean one, and three runs is the floor rather than a comfortable sample.

cases.prompt: One of my skills has never fired once. Is its description wrong?
cases.why: sits inside skill-authoring's 'how to word a description so it triggers'; the ask is diagnosis

cases.prompt: I rewrote a skill's description. How do I know the new wording is actually better than the old one?
cases.why: candidate scoring; 'rewrote a description' is authoring vocabulary throughout

cases.prompt: Two of my skills keep getting picked for the same kind of request. Which one is winning?
cases.why: contention, and both descriptions name the situation

cases.prompt: This skill has grown to cover three different things. Is it worth breaking up?
cases.why: splitting an over-scoped skill is fitness', but reads like an authoring decision

cases.prompt: I edited a SKILL.md an hour ago and my session still behaves like the old version.
cases.why: source versus installed copy; 'skill behaves wrongly' is fitness-shaped phrasing

cases.prompt: Help me word this new skill's description so it doesn't poach requests from my other ones.
cases.why: composition, not diagnosis - the mirror of case 1 and the case most likely to go wrong

cases.prompt: I want to publish my skills so a teammate can install them from GitHub.
cases.why: publishing and installation are authoring's; nothing here is measurable

cases.prompt: Should this convention be its own skill, or just a rule in AGENTS.md?
cases.why: authoring owns 'when something should be an instructions-file rule instead of a skill at all'

cases.prompt: Add a task to this repo's tasks.py that rebuilds the docs, and name it properly.
cases.why: should-not-steal: an ordinary request neither meta-skill may take

cases.prompt: What's a good way to structure the tests for this Python package?
cases.why: should-not-steal: 'structure' and 'package' are ordinary words both meta-skills share
